question.text: The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find $h'(3)$ where $h(x)=f(x)+g(x).$
question.explanation:
The addition rule for derivatives gives

\[ h'(x) =f'(x) + g'(x). \]

As a result, we have that

\[ h'(3) = f'(3) + g'(3). \]

Also, notice that $x=3$ corresponds to

  • the interval $x\in(2,4)$ for the function $f,$ and

  • the interval $x\in(2.5,4)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

  • The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in(2,4)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{0-2}{4-2} = -1. \] Therefore, $f'(3)=-1.$

  • The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in(2.5,4)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{1-1}{4-2.5} = 0. \] Therefore, $g'(3)=0.$

Finally, we have

\begin{align*} h'\left(3\right) &= f'\left(3\right) + g'\left(3\right) \\[5pt] &= -1 + 0 \\[5pt] &= -1. \end{align*}

question.text: Given the plots of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ above, find $h'(4)$ where $h(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}.$
question.explanation:
The quotient rule for derivatives gives

\[ h'(x) = \dfrac{f'(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot g'(x)}{(g(x))^2}. \]

As a result, we have that

\[ h'(4) = \dfrac{f'(4)\cdot g(4)-f(4)\cdot g'(4)}{(g(4))^2}. \]

From the graph above, we obtain that $f\left(4\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $g\left(4\right)=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$

Additionally:

  • The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in(3,5)$ equals $-\dfrac{3}{2}.$ So, $f'\left(4\right)=-\dfrac{3}{2}.$

  • The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in\left(\dfrac{7}{2},5\right)$ equals $1.$ So, $g'\left(4\right)=1.$

Finally, we have

\begin{align*} h'\left(4\right) &= \dfrac{f'\left(4\right)\cdot g\left(4\right)-f\left(4\right)\cdot g'\left(4\right)}{\left(g\left(4\right)\right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1}{\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)} \\[5pt] &= 1. \end{align*}

question.text: Given the plots of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ above, find $h'(-3)$ where $h(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}.$
question.explanation:
The quotient rule for derivatives gives

\[ h'(x) = \dfrac{f'(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot g'(x)}{(g(x))^2}. \]

As a result, we have that

\[ h'(-3) = \dfrac{f'(-3)\cdot g(-3)-f(-3)\cdot g'(-3)}{(g(-3))^2}. \]

From the graph above, we obtain that $f(-3)=-1$ and $g(-3)=-2.$

Additionally:

  • The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in(-4,0)$ equals $1.$ So, $f'(-3)=1.$

  • The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in(-4,4)$ equals $0.$ So, $g'(-3)=0.$

Finally, we have

\begin{align*} h'(-3) &= \dfrac{f'(-3)\cdot g(-3)-f(-3)\cdot g'(-3)}{(g(-3))^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1 \cdot (-2) - (-1) \cdot0}{(-2)^2} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align*}

question.text: The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find $p'(1.5)$ where $p(x)=f(x)g(x).$
question.explanation:
The product rule for derivatives gives \[ p'(x)=f'(x)\cdot g(x)+f(x)\cdot g'(x). \]

As a result, we have that \[ p'(1.5)=f'(1.5)\cdot g(1.5)+f(1.5)\cdot g'(1.5). \]

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(1.5)=-2$ and $g(1.5)=-0.5.$

Additionally,

  • The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in(1,3)$ equals $1.$ So, $f'(1.5)=1.$

  • The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in(1,3)$ equals $1.$ So, $g'(1.5)=1.$

Therefore, \begin{align*} p'(1.5)&=f'(1.5) \cdot g(1.5)+f(1.5)\cdot g'(1.5) \\[5pt] &= 1\cdot (-0.5) + (-2)\cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-2.5}. \end{align*}
